title: Health, Items and Inventory
summary: Combat and loot turn Delve into a game. This lesson adds health and attack components, a damage formula with a little randomness, death and drops, item definitions loaded from data, pickups, and an inventory where identical items **stack**. Every number lives in a data file, so balancing never needs a rebuild.
markdown:
## Components for combat

Following lesson 10.03, combat is a few components and one system:

```cpp-norun
struct Health   { int current; int maximum; };
struct Attack   { int power; int accuracy; };      // accuracy: chance to hit, in percent
struct Defence  { int armour; };
struct Drops    { std::string itemId; int chance; };  // percent
```

The player and every monster have `Health`, `Attack` and `Defence`; values come from `monsters.ini` (lesson 10.08), so a troll is just a different set of numbers.

## The damage formula

When an attacker hits a defender:

1. **Roll to hit**: a random number from 1 to 100; it hits if the roll is at most the attacker's accuracy.
2. **Damage**: `power − armour / 2`, plus a small random spread (−1 to +1), but **at least 1** so every hit matters.
3. Subtract from the defender's health; at 0 or below, the defender dies.

```cpp-norun
int rollDamage(const Attack& a, const Defence& d, Random& rng)
{
    if (rng.range(1, 100) > a.accuracy) return 0;             // a miss
    const int base{ a.power - d.armour / 2 };
    return std::max(1, base + rng.range(-1, 1));
}
```

Two habits make combat code easy to balance and test:

- **One random number generator object**, passed in, never `rand()` scattered around. Seed it from the time in normal play and from a fixed number for tests and replays (lesson 10.02's determinism).
- **Log every combat event** to the message log (lesson 8.03's ring buffer, shown on screen): "The goblin hits you for 3. (HP 17/20)". Players need the feedback, and you need it to see whether the numbers feel right.

## Death and drops

When a monster dies, the combat system removes its entity (lesson 3.10's handles mean nothing else is left pointing at it) and, according to its `Drops` component, may place an item on its tile. The player dying ends the run with a "you died" screen showing the last few log lines, so the player knows why.

## Items from data

```ini
; items.ini
[potion]
name = Healing potion
heal = 10
stack = 5

[dagger]
name = Rusty dagger
power = 2
stack = 1

[gold]
name = Gold coins
stack = 999
```

An item **definition** (the data) is shared; an item in the world or inventory is just a definition id and a count. That keeps inventories small and makes "how many potions do I have?" a lookup.

## The inventory

The inventory is a fixed number of **slots** (say 10). Each slot holds an item id and a count, up to that item's stack limit. Picking up items:

1. First top up existing slots of the same item, up to the stack limit.
2. Then put the rest into empty slots.
3. Whatever does not fit stays on the floor.

```
picking up 7 potions (stack 5) with slots:  [potion 4] [dagger 1] [empty] [empty]
→ [potion 5] [dagger 1] [potion 5] [potion 1]      nothing left over
```

Using an item removes one from its slot, and an empty slot becomes free. The practice task implements adding and removing with exactly these rules, which is the part most likely to hide off-by-one bugs.

## Common mistakes

> [!warning] Damage that can be zero or negative
> High armour should reduce damage, not heal the target. Clamp to at least 1 on a hit.

> [!warning] Calling `rand()` everywhere
> Use one seeded generator object so tests and replays are repeatable.

> [!warning] Copying item definitions into every slot
> Store an id and a count; look the definition up when needed.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What are the steps of the damage formula?
- Damage is always the attacker's power; armour is ignored
- Subtract armour from health, then roll to see if the attack missed
+ Roll to hit, then power minus half armour plus spread, at least 1
- Multiply power by armour, divide by the defender's health
> Clamping to at least 1 means a hit always does something, however strong the armour.

? What is the difference between an item definition and an item in the inventory?
+ A definition is shared data; a slot holds just its id and count
- The definition is in the inventory; the item is on the floor
- They are the same struct, copied into each slot
- The definition is C++ code; the item is a script
> Sharing one definition means changing a potion in the data file changes every potion.

? In what order does picking up fill the inventory?
- Empty slots first, then existing stacks
- Only empty slots; stacks are never topped up
+ Top up matching stacks, then use empty slots
- The item replaces whatever is in the first slot
> Topping up stacks first keeps empty slots free for as long as possible; whatever does not fit stays on the floor.

? Why clamp damage to at least 1 on a hit?
+ So every hit matters, and never heals
- To make the game easier
- Because health cannot be negative
> Without it, high armour makes damage zero or negative.

? Why pass a random generator object around instead of calling `rand()`?
- `rand()` does not exist in C++
+ It can be seeded, so tests and replays repeat
- It is always faster
> Determinism needs control over the random numbers.

? An inventory has [potion 4] and one empty slot; potions stack to 5. Seven potions are picked up. What happens?
- All seven fit in the first slot
- The pickup fails
+ Slots become 5 and 5; 1 stays on the floor
> Top up existing stacks first, then fill empty slots, and leave the rest.
```
ideas:
- Put combat into Delve and tune the goblin until fighting two at once is dangerous but winnable.
- Seed the generator with a fixed number and check that the same moves give the same fight every time.
- Show the inventory as a row of boxes at the bottom of the screen with each slot's count.
